notes: The keyboard, properly this time. From Android 15 the phone stopped resizing the app when the keys appear and simply lays them over the bottom of it, so the app now shortens its own page above the keys - the same thing older Android did for it. The line you are on stays in sight with a line of air beneath it.
This one is in the app itself, not only in the page: install the new APK from the releases page for it to take effect. The notes you already have stay exactly where they are.

The keyboard, properly this time. From Android 15 the phone stopped resizing the app when the keys appear and simply lays them over the bottom of it, so the app now shortens its own page above the keys - the same thing older Android did for it. The line you are on stays in sight with a line of air beneath it.
This one is in the app itself, not only in the page: install the new APK from the releases page for it to take effect. The notes you already have stay exactly where they are.
The keyboard no longer covers the note. The page now ends where the keys begin instead of running on underneath them, so the toolbar, the word count and the last line all stay in sight.
The line you are typing keeps a line of air above the keys rather than sitting against them, the way an OxygenOS note does, and the bottom rail steps out of the way while the keys are up.

history.title: Every app on the shelf opens, and a tidier page
notes: Every app on the shelf opens when it is tapped, not only the small Open button in the corner of its row: the whole row is the link now, and it dips under the finger like the rest of the app.

The line of small print under the recent notes is gone. The three buttons at the top of the page share their row instead of leaving Search sitting on its own under a gap, and Other apps is at the foot of the page where it can be found without going into Settings.

history.title: The keyboard stops covering the note
notes: The keyboard no longer sits on top of what you are writing. The app draws to the whole screen and the phone lays its keys over the bottom of that, so the writing box kept its full height behind them and the line being typed was underneath, out of sight and impossible to scroll to. The page now measures the part of the screen the keys are covering and keeps the note above it, and it nudges the caret back into view as the box gets shorter.
Only while a field is focused: a pinch zoom or the browser's own bar sliding away is not treated as a keyboard, and the sheet for a rename or a PIN stays above the keys too.

history.title: Patch notes are the ones the page is running
notes: The patch notes were read from the file beside the page, and in the installed app the page is served from the copy that came inside the APK, so the list stopped at the version the APK was built with: after taking a page over the air it sat behind the running app, with no mark on the release that was actually on screen. The notes now come from the same place the update check comes from, so the newest release is at the top and the one you are on says so.
With no network the notes fall back to the copy that came with the app, and say that is what they are instead of looking out of date.

history.title: The pad keeps its own long press, and answers at once
notes: A long press is the app's own again. Holding a key on the PIN pad used to bring Android's Copy, Share and Select all menu down over the pad, with a pair of selection handles sitting on the keys; nothing on the app's own screen is text to select now, which also keeps a two second hold on a note a hold on a note. The words inside a note, and the text you type, are still selectable and copyable.
The pad answers under the finger instead of after it: a key dips as it is pressed, and taps are no longer held back while the browser waits to see whether a second one is coming.

A dot pops as it fills, and a wrong PIN shakes the dots and the keys as well as turning the message red, then clears the entry so the next try starts from nothing. Every one of those moves is off when the phone asks for reduced motion.

history.title: Several notes at once, a page to land on, and ink that curves
notes: More than one note at a time: hold a note in the list for two seconds and a ring closes around the row - then every tap adds or removes a note from the selection, and the bar that appears acts on all of them at once. Star them, move them into a folder, put them in the Vault, or send them to the trash together. The back button or the x in the bar lets go. A finger that starts scrolling before the ring closes was scrolling, not holding, so nothing is selected by accident.

The app no longer opens on the note at the top of the list. It lands on a page of its own: a greeting, how many notes you have and when the last one was written, New note, Today and Search, the notes you were last in, and the ones you pinned. Nothing is open until you open it, so launch cannot put somebody else's words in front of you again.

Handwriting is drawn as the curve the pen actually described rather than as straight pieces between the points it reported. The line is resampled about every page unit, so a quick stroke curls instead of cornering, and the width eases from one sample to the next, so pressing harder thickens the line smoothly instead of in steps. The page also reads a stylus's raw updates where the phone offers them, which keeps the shape of a fast hand. Old drawings are painted by the same code, so they look better too.

A drawing can now be part of the note it was drawn in. Add to note, at the right of the pen bar, paints the page onto a picture with the note's own colours behind it (so it reads in either theme, and is sealed with the note when the note is in the Vault), writes it into the note's text where any other picture goes, then clears the page so the next drawing starts empty. Undo brings the strokes back if you change your mind.

The pieces of the page move instead of jumping: a sheet settles in and fades behind it, a pane lifts a couple of pixels when it changes, the selection bar slides up, rows and buttons press when a finger lands on them, and the drawing and the pictures fade in as they arrive. All of that turns itself off when the phone asks for less motion.

The launcher icon on the home screen is the artwork the Play listing shows, at last: the small u at the foot of the page is a letter rather than two circles and a slit, and the mark is the same size inside Android's 72dp safe window as it is in the listing's own picture. My Hub draws the app's icon straight from the phone, so its row follows from the same fix.

history.title: The links graph stops sitting under the clock
notes: The links graph covers the whole screen, so it used to start at the very top of it and draw its own header — "How your notes connect" and the Close button — straight under the clock. It now keeps clear of the phone's bars like every other surface, and its header is one tidy row: the title gives way with an ellipsis instead of wrapping over the legend, and the Close button has room.

history.title: A guaranteed gap at the top, and a way back out
notes: The top of the page always keeps a status bar's worth of room above it now, whether or not the phone tells the page how tall that bar is. A WebView that reports nothing used to leave the Write/Read/Draw switch and the buttons beside it drawn on top of the clock; now a phone always starts 36 pixels down, and a real measurement from the phone wins whenever it is bigger. That is a guaranteed gap rather than a hope.

There is a Back button in the top bar, on the left, and it appears whenever there is somewhere to go back to: the search or the command palette, a sheet, the note list drawer, a tag or folder filter, the Vault, the Trash. On a phone it takes the menu button's place while it is showing, so nothing is crowded.

The search and the command palette have a back arrow of their own in their header, which is the way out that was missing: before, the only exit was the phone's back key, and that left the app entirely.

The phone's back key does the same as the arrow now: it closes the sheet, the search, the graph or the drawer in front of it, then lets go of a filter, and only closes the app when there is nothing left to close.

history.title: Folded, unfolded, flipped, on its side
notes: The page now lays itself out for the shape of the screen it is on, not just its width. A folded foldable and a phone keep the drawer and the row of buttons at the bottom; an unfolded foldable or a small tablet gets the rail and the note list as a column of their own, with the note beside them instead of behind a button; a tablet or a desktop window also gets the links pane back, and the writing column stops widening and sits in the middle, so a line of text stays a line of text instead of running the whole way across.

A flip's cover screen, and any phone held sideways, get a short-screen layout: the word count bar at the bottom gives way first, the title and the margins shrink, the top bar gets shorter and the row of buttons at the bottom drops to 50 pixels, so the note itself keeps the room.
On the narrowest covers one row of controls has to do: the search box gives way, the buttons tighten, and the dialogs and the PIN pad lose their side margins rather than their buttons.

Folding and unfolding no longer restarts the page. The app now handles a change of smallest size and of pixel density itself, the way it already handled a rotation, so the note you had open is the note you still have open when the screen grows or folds.

history.title: The bar below the status bar, on every phone
notes: The top of the page sits below the status bar on every phone now. The page was written to keep clear of the phone's own bars, and a browser tells it how tall they are - but an Android WebView reports nothing at all, so inside the app the first row of the screen was drawn under the clock: the Write/Read/Draw switch and the buttons beside it ended up on top of the time and the battery. The app now measures the status bar, the notch, the navigation bar and the keyboard itself and hands those heights to the page, so the two copies lay themselves out the same way on a small phone, a tall one, a phone with a cutout, and with three buttons or a gesture bar at the bottom. The heights are measured again on a rotation and whenever the keyboard opens, so nothing goes stale.
The bottom of the page keeps its own margin once, not twice: the content area no longer adds the navigation bar on top of the page's own padding. Nothing else about the notebook changes.

history.title: A backup that carries the Vault, and a screen that clears the bars
notes: A backup is the whole notebook now. Notes, folders, tags, settings, pictures, recordings and the Vault travel together: every Vault note goes into the file sealed, with the salt and the verifier that were made from your PIN, so the PIN you already had is the PIN that opens them on the other side. Anything written while the Vault was locked went with the file too, which used to be the one thing a backup left behind.

Import puts the Vault back where it belongs. The sealed notes go into the Vault and wait there, locked, until you type the PIN they were sealed with - they no longer come back as untitled strays in the note list or in the Trash. A backup from an older version that carried its sealed records among the plain notes is sorted out on the way in, and any such strays already on the phone are moved into the Vault once, on launch.
If this phone already has a Vault of its own, with notes inside it and a different PIN, that Vault is left exactly as it was and the app says so, instead of quietly dropping the one in the backup.
The welcome sheet offers Import a backup. A new phone can be set up from the file before a single note is written - the notes arrive where they were, and the Vault is waiting behind its PIN.

The top of the page keeps clear of the status bar and the notch, and the row of buttons at the bottom keeps clear of the navigation bar, in the app and in the copy installed from the browser. The bar along the top is taller with room to tap, the sheet's buttons wrap instead of crowding, and a dialog can never grow past the screen it is on.

history.title: A build a store will take, and the bars back in place
notes: The version on the app and the version on the page are the same number now. It was typed twice - 1.0.16 in the build, whatever the page said in updates.json - so the APK could call itself a release the notebook had already moved past. The build reads the page's own number, and the version code is worked out from it: 1.0.19 is 1000019, and it can only go up.
The app targets Android 16 now, which is what a new listing on Play has to do from 31 August 2026. Nothing about the notebook changes because of it.

On Android 15 and later the phone draws apps behind the status bar and the row of navigation buttons, and this page was written to sit between them - so the first line of the screen and the buttons at the bottom would have slipped underneath. Where the phone insists, the heights of those two bars are added back as space, and the keyboard's height with them.
The release itself is a bundle now as well as an APK, both signed with the same upload key, both built from the same commit. Nothing to install differently: the APK is still the one for a phone.

history.title: A privacy policy of its own, linked from Settings
notes: UNote has a privacy policy. It lives at anekthegreat.github.io/UNote/privacy.html and is linked from Settings, under About, so what the app keeps and what it does with it is one tap from inside the app rather than a page you have to be told about.

It says what is true of this app in plain words: your notes, drawings, pictures and recordings are kept in the app's own storage on the phone; a Vault note is encrypted on the phone with a key made from your PIN, with nothing of the PIN stored; backups and transfer codes are made only when you ask and go only where you send them.

It also names the one thing that leaves the phone - the check for a newer copy of the app's own interface, from this project's GitHub Pages site - and what GitHub sees when that happens. There is no account, no analytics, no advertising and no third-party library in the app, and the page says so.

history.title: Handwriting: draw on a note with a pen or a stylus
notes: Handwriting. A note has a Draw pane now, beside Write, Split and Read: a page you write on with a finger, a stylus or a mouse. It sits under the same title as the words, so one note can hold a shopping list and a scribbled diagram.

Seven colours and three widths, an eraser, undo and redo, and a Clear that asks twice. The first colour is the text colour itself, so a drawing is readable in the dark theme and the light one without picking a colour at all. Ctrl/Cmd+Z undoes a stroke while the Draw pane is on screen.

A stylus is treated like a pen. Pressing harder draws a thicker line, a fast line keeps every point the pen reported instead of cutting the corners, and once the stylus has been seen a finger touching the screen within a second and a half is taken for a hand resting on it and ignored. The eraser end of a stylus erases.

The ink is part of the note, not a picture beside it. It is saved the same way the words are, it travels in a backup and in a transfer code, and a note in the Vault has its ink sealed with it. A note with a drawing shows a small pen in the list and a Handwriting tag above the page.

history.title: The Vault stops losing notes
notes: The Vault no longer loses a note to locking. When it locks, the note you had open is written first, so the last thing you typed is still there when you come back.

Words typed while the Vault was locked are kept. A save that could not be encrypted used to be dropped in silence, which is how the end of a note could vanish after the automatic lock. It now waits on the phone and is saved the moment your PIN is back.
Moving a note into the Vault writes it once, complete. The old code wrote an empty sealed record first, and a note caught in that moment could never be read again.
A star on a Vault note now survives a lock, like every other note.
If sealed notes are on this phone but the record that checks the PIN is missing, the app says so instead of offering a new PIN that would bury them for good.
Less nagging: the Vault no longer shuts itself while a Vault note is open, and the side bar says how many notes are sealed behind the lock.

history.title: What's new stops coming back
notes: What's new no longer opens by itself on every launch. It opens once, and only for a version that is really newer than the last one this phone showed you.

Two everyday things used to bring it back: the app serving an older page than the one inside the APK, which made the version differ in both directions, and closing the app while the sheet was open, which counted as never having read it. The mark is written the moment the sheet appears, and it never moves backwards.
The welcome screen is remembered the same way, so it cannot return for the same reason.
The notes are still one tap away: What's new in the footer, and Patch notes in Settings.

history.title: A new build takes effect immediately
notes: Installing a newer APK now takes effect straight away. The app keeps the page it downloaded last time in its own storage and was serving that instead of the page inside the new APK, so a fresh install could keep opening the old version and look like nothing had changed.
An out-of-date downloaded page is dropped automatically, and only a page newer than the app itself is ever served.
Settings now says whether this screen is the page that came inside the app or one fetched earlier, so a shadowed page is visible instead of mysterious.

history.title: Attachments open, read mode shows the note
notes: Photos, videos and audio files now open the phone's own picker. The app was asking the page for a file but never opening anything, so tapping the attachment button did nothing at all.
A voice memo can start: the microphone request is answered by the app, and the permission is in the manifest.
Pictures can be pasted straight into a note, including a picture copied as an image in another app.
There is an "Any file" row for documents and PDFs, and several files can be picked at once.
Read mode shows the note: the reading pane now fills its row instead of collapsing to nothing, re-renders when you switch to it, and falls back to plain text rather than showing an empty page.

history.title: The update check tries, and says what it did
notes: The update check tries again instead of giving up. It used to ask once, a second after the app opened - often before the phone had a signal - and say nothing if that failed.
It now retries a few times, and checks again every time you come back to the app.
When there is nothing newer, a quiet "Up to date" shows for a few seconds, so you can see the check ran instead of hoping it did.
Settings reports the last check in words: the time, whether it got through, which version the site offers - or why it did not get through.

history.title: Updates that arrive on their own
notes: The installed app updates itself now. It asks the UNote site once at launch, and when there is a newer version a chip says so: one tap fetches it, keeps it inside the app and reopens on it. No store, no APK to download, nothing to install.
The app asks the network for exactly two things: that update file, and the page when you take an update. Notes, the Vault, backups and attachments still never leave the phone.
Settings has one way back: "Go back to the built-in version" throws away a fetched page and returns to the copy that came inside the APK.
This is the one version that still has to be installed by hand - the version before it had no way to hear about updates. After this, the fixes arrive on their own.

history.title: A PIN with no keyboard, and backups that land
notes: Setting a Vault PIN uses the number pad now, the same one that unlocks it. No keyboard opens, so nothing offers to save or fill a password over the PIN.
Backups work inside the app: saving one asks the phone where to keep it, and choosing one to import opens the phone file picker - which never opened before.
A file the phone labels unknown is no longer hidden from the picker.
The graph is titled what it shows, says how many notes and links it drew, and when there are none it says how to make one: write [[another note's title]].

history.title: Photos, voice memos, and a calmer page
notes: Photos, video, audio and voice memos go into a note now. Paste one in, pick one from the phone, or record a memo and it lands in the page with a player.
Anything added to a note in the Vault is sealed with the Vault's key, like the words. Close the Vault and it goes from the page too.
A transfer carries them: the file export includes every attachment. A Vault that arrives from another phone opens only with the PIN it was sealed with - the old one - or you reset it and start empty.
A calmer surface: one soft wash instead of three, more room around the writing, plainer note details, and a phone opens into the page instead of three cramped panes.

history.title: The Vault is a room, and a way back in
notes: The Vault is a room now, not a filter. Its notes are only in front of you while you are inside it.
Close the Vault and it locks: no Vault title, tag, link or count shows anywhere else - not in search, the graph, or the note list.
Reset the Vault: from Settings or from the PIN screen. It says what a reset does, offers to save the notes as a text file first, and lets you set a new PIN straight away.

history.title: A welcome, not a PIN
notes: The start is a welcome now: what UNote is, and one button that begins a note. It no longer opens by asking for a Vault PIN.
The Vault is a choice, not a step. It asks for its PIN the first time you open it, which is when the PIN means something.
The first note is short: tap it and type, how to link two notes, how to tag one, and where the Vault is.

history.title: All five rows answer
notes: Other apps still lists the same five apps, in the same order, with the same lines.
My Hub and UJournal pointed at a repository page rather than the release a build installs from. Both now open the release, and MeasureT opens its page.
SideCut keeps its Play listing, which is the only listing in the family that is live.

history.title: Liquid glass, and the rest of the shelf
notes: Liquid glass: every panel, card and sheet is now a pane with a soft edge, a blur behind it and a line of light along the top, so the app reads as one surface instead of a stack of boxes.
Other apps: a new list - FamTM, SideCut, MeasureT, My Hub and UJournal - each with one honest line about it and one tap to open it. It sits in the footer and in Settings.
Calmer controls: rounder buttons, softer rows, a clearer accent, and the text size and accent colour you pick are still yours.
A link in that list opens in the phone browser or the Play Store and comes back to the note you were on; the app itself still asks the network for nothing.

history.title: A fuller mark, and no black disc
notes: The icon is redrawn: the note card now fills the icon instead of sitting inside a black circle at the bottom right.
The two link dots rest on the card and part along a hairline, so the only dark line left is a hair thin one.
Adaptive, round, themed and home-screen icons are redrawn together, so the APK and the installed page match.

history.title: Patch notes, and an icon with some thought in it
notes: Patch notes: a What's new button sits in the footer, and Settings has a row for it. Every version is listed, newest first.
After an over-the-air update the sheet opens once by itself, so a new version says what changed instead of just being newer.
A new launcher icon: a note card with a folded corner on a violet field, with an adaptive, a round and a themed version for Android.

history.title: The line above the note keeps up
notes: The title line above a note follows the title, the word count and the reading time as you type.

history.title: Creating the Vault is one form
notes: Creating the Vault is one form: type the PIN, type it again, done, instead of two dialogs in a row that could lose the second half.

history.title: The first release
notes: Notes with markdown, folders, tags, [[links]] with backlinks, a graph, and search on Ctrl+K.
A Vault behind a PIN you choose, encrypted on the device, that locks itself and can change its PIN.
Export everything to one file, carry it as a code, import it back.
Offline first, and it can be installed to a home screen.
